newsitem.title: FRANCE: French consumer confidence up after Socialist win.
newsitem.headline: French consumer confidence up after Socialist win.

text.p: French consumer confidence rose sharply in June after the Socialists were elected to power on promises to promote jobs and economic growth, but economists are skeptical that the improvement signals a lasting change.

Statistics institute INSEE's overall confidence indicator increased 10 points last month to minus 23 from minus 33 in May, hitting its highest level in two years, figures on Wednesday released by the government agency showed.
The seasonally adjusted findings indicated fewer respondents were pessimistic about their future than in the previous month.
Economists said that if the upturn were confirmed by higher spending, it could provide a welcome boost to economic growth which has been hobbled by weak consumer demand.

The confidence indicator stood at its highest level in June since the minus 21 attained in August 1995, soon after conservative Jacques Chirac was elected president -- also on a pledge to bring down unemployment.
INSEE economist Alain Chappert said there was normally a rise in consumer confidence after an election.
The improvement this time was sharper than after elections in 1993 and 1995. But private economists were reluctant to say the survey marked a sea change.

"We have seen this before. After elections, people tend to believe things will be all right and that unemployment will be attacked, and then we have seen confidence fall again," said economist Philippe Brossard of ABN-Amro Finance.

Economists suggested the findings probably reflected Socialist campaign promises to put job creation and growth at the top of the political agenda and to achieve European monetary union without further belt-tightening.

Despite economists' forecasts that the jobless rate will stay around a near record 12.5 percent for the rest of 1997, respondents were particularly optimistic about future unemployment levels, with confidence climbing a hefty 27 points.
The survey, which samples the views of 2,000 households, is a fairly volatile indicator and has been an unreliable tool of late to forecast spending plans, economists said.
Economist Stuart Thomson of Credit Agricole Indosuez said he still expected household consumption figures for June to show a drop for the second straight month.

"It's a bit too early to be sure (of an improvement)," said Brossard of ABN-AMRO. He said talk of a big budget deficit for 1997, the crucial qualifying year for monetary union, "is going to depress people again."
